title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: Data
text:
Data

Synthetic Population Catalyst (SPC)–A synthetic population that simulates individual-level travel behavior (home and workplace), travel mode, demographic and socio-economic characteristics that allow us to explore heat vulnerability at the individual level
Tube operation timetable–For travel times and route estimation, we use the timetable provided by Transport for London (TfL) APIs. Provides accurate estimation whether travelers for each OD-pair will take air-conditioned Tube lines

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: 1. Estimate Tube travellers
text: 1. Estimate Tube travellers

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: Synthetic Population Catalyst Project
text: Synthetic Population Catalyst Project

title: Mind the Temperatures:
text:
Start with SPC: individual-level estimates for a range of demographic and socioeconomic attributes, including health, household composition, employment status
Incorporate Office of National Statistics (ONS) projections for future population scenarios
Place individuals within Output Areas: the smallest UK census geographical units
Also combine SPC home and work locations with data from the National Travel Survey (NTS) to estimate travel mode
Which gives us estimates of individuals (with characteristics) for 2019 and 2039

Mostly working age

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: 2. Simulate journeys
text: 2. Simulate journeys

title: Mind the Temperatures:
text:
We identify subway commuters from the synthetic population with the National Travel Survey
Travel routes are assumed from/to the nearest Tube stations of their origin and destination Output Area and mapped to the London Tube network built from the operating timetable published by TfL
Shortest path line-specific on-board travel times and transit waiting times are derived at the station‐to‐station level

If more than one station is available and the distance difference is less than 500m, the station with the shortest travel time on the network is picked

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: 3. Calculate journey temperatures
text: 3. Calculate journey temperatures

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: Climate data
text:
Climate data

Above-ground temperature data: Convection Permitting Model (CPM), part of UK Climate Projections 2018 (UKCP18), published by the UK Met Office

This is UKCP18’s finest spatial resolution of climate model (2.2km grid)

We use 2019 daily high-temperature data to represent the current situation and to calculate heat exposure
For future scenarios, we combine the 5-year projection data from 2037-2042, sorting the days by temperature across years, then generating a synthetic year ranked by high temperature

title: Mind the Temperatures:
text:
In 2019, the average summer day high temperature was 23.36 °C

By 2039, that rises to 26.24 °C, indicating an increase of nearly 3 °C for average summer highs.

In 2019, the hottest day reached 29.76 °C

By 2039, the peak climbs to 35.38 °C

Largest differences between the future and baseline curves are often observed during summer peaks

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: Estimating journey temperatures
text:
Estimating journey temperatures

Station and journey segments are linked to the above-ground temperature data
Station‐level temperatures–the sum of surface temperatures and line-specific temperature offsets derived from TfL data indicating how much warmer or cooler the train line is relative to the surface
Journey segment temperatures–the average of origin and destination station temperatures

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: Creating heat exposure indicators
text:
Creating heat exposure indicators

Calculated by combining temperature values with the corresponding travel times (on-board) and transfer times (while waiting at stations)

Total Degree Minutes (TDM)–capturing cumulative thermal stress as the time‐temperature product, where longer exposure at higher temperatures yields larger values
Extreme Degree Minutes (EDM)–quantifying total time spent in extremely hot environments (above 30 °C), potentially linked to acute health risks

title: Mind the Temperatures:
text:
By matching station-to-station heat exposure from home locations to work locations provided from commuting journeys, we can estimate individual-level heat exposure along with individual characteristics
Network‐level heat exposure is obtained by summing or averaging Origin‐Destination (OD) pair‐specific indicators across the entire Tube system, yielding heat exposure indicators for the London Underground System
We define the following as vulnerable: BMI>35 or having either diabetes, high blood pressure, or cardiovascular diseases
387,876 London residents (mainly working age) were included in the analysis, with an average daily travel time of 28.01 minutes (2019)

title: Mind the Temperatures:
text:
2019

For all residents, the mean Total Degree Minutes (TDM) on a typical day was 761.98, rising to 881.10 degree*mins on the hottest day
Findings indicate the risk sharply increases on hot days: both TDM and EDM jump considerably from the average day to the hottest day

title: Mind the Temperatures:
text:
2039

Average travel time of 28.45 minutes–slightly longer than the 28.01 minutes observed in 2019
Both Total Degree‐Minutes (TDM) and Extreme Degree Minutes (EDM) are forecast to rise for all groups compared with 2019
Among all residents, the mean TDM on a typical day increases from 761.98 in 2019 to 816.39 in 2039, while on the hottest day, it grows from 881.10 to 919.19.
EDM on an average day nearly doubles, from 5.77 to 12.53. The hottest‐day increase is more modest (17.30 to 17.60).

Almost all deep Tube lines in 2019 exceeded the extreme threshold we set on the hottest day, so even if the temperature for the hottest days is much higher in 2039, there is not much space for EDM to increase

title: Mind the Temperatures:
text:
Certain areas of Greater London—especially in the northeast and, to a lesser degree, in the southern boroughs—bear considerably higher heat exposure burdens
Confluence of spatial inequality and population vulnerability, with disadvantaged communities facing longer or more intense heat exposure when travelling on deep Tube lines, especially Central and Northern Lines
Heightened exposures coincide with populations who may have limited capacity to cope, due to factors such as restricted travel options, lack of air‐conditioned alternatives, or an elevated baseline risk of heat‐related illness

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: 1: Drivers of inequality in heat exposure
text:
1: Drivers of inequality in heat exposure

Clear geographical variations in heat exposure for Tube travelers in both time periods

Would be interesting to allocate travelers to specific lines to estimate population (and neighborhood) benefits of installing AC
Would also be helpful to look at neighborhood characteristics

Peripheral areas have notably higher levels of “extreme minutes” and “total temperature minutes”

These disparities are still more pronounced in future projections for 2039, suggesting that existing inequalities may deepen with ongoing climate change

title: Mind the Temperatures:
section: What’s driving this observed geographic unevenness?
text:
What’s driving this observed geographic unevenness?

Infrastructure and line characteristics:

Older, deeper lines are prone to higher on-board temperatures
Areas dependent on these lines (e.g., those lying along certain radial routes) show higher overall exposure

Journey length:

Outer London residents accumulate much more heat exposure compared to central London residents
Many of these areas have fewer transport alternatives—-particularly air‐conditioned services

title: Why Digital Twins Matter (Do They?)
text:
Need: They fill a gap!
Physical Foundations: They foreground the physical components of cities (like transport networks and the built and natural environments)
Efficiency: Yay efficiency!
Scenarios: They open the door to richer what-if scenario testing.
Uncertainty: They can help reinforce the importance of model uncertainty
Appeal: It’s rare a modelling framework or paradigm attaches itself so firmly and so widely to such a variety of domains (public, private, academic) and areas (infrastructure, land use, transport). This is not to be discounted lightly.

title: Why Digital Twins Matter (Do They?)
section: Just kidding
text: Just kidding

title: Why Digital Twins Matter (Do They?)
section: No but really
text:
No but really

Lack of demographic, economic, and social process: They ‘rarely include any of the processes that determine how the city works in terms of its social and economic functions’ (Batty, 2018).
Society at Scale: What does a social DT look like? How can individuals, communities, and policies be captured and presented in a DT?
Mutability: When urban physical systems change, the sources of that change are typically straightforward to identify. Humans are more difficult.
Scalability: Wicked societal problems are wicked because they are complex and big
Time horizons: City DTs and other DTs work at a time scale consisting of minutes, days, and months, using real-time data to fine-tune immediate responses. This is not the time scale of wicked urban and social problems
Technocracy: The greatest risk that DTs pose may be precisely what makes them so popular: the promise that they are a panacea for a range of challenges that other approaches – and policy and investment – have failed to resolve.

title: Why Digital Twins Matter (Do They?)
text:
Data, compute, and real time aren’t going anywhere
Reckoning with data (access, bias, privacy) also isn’t going anywhere
Rallying points are valuable (this is kind of a big deal)
Digital Twins try to respond to a clearly identified need/gap (also a big deal)

Where you convince yourself and others of the what, why, and how of your research
This is three parts motivation, justification, and promotion

Literature Review/Background
Data and Methods—These elements are like a recipe; can someone cook the same research meal from your description?
Analysis and Discussion—Not only what you did (the analysis), but what you found!
Conclusions—Brief synopsis of what you’ve done, but mostly main takeaways (main findings, contribution to the literature, policy relevance, caveats, future research)

title: Literature Reviews:
section: There’s no one right way to do a literature review
text:
There’s no one right way to do a literature review

The more you read and the more you practice, the more you see there are lots of ways to successfully write a scientific work
The internet is useful for all things academic!

Read and discard what doesn’t apply to you

I find it most helpful to think of the literature review as a process, one that you undergo for your own understanding of a topic
Once that’s settled in your mind, the writing and the structure will come more easily

title: Literature Reviews:
section: What purpose does it serve?
text:
What purpose does it serve?

A literature review synthesizes and assesses what we know about a topic and how we know it
And also sketches out a place for the research you are about to describe

This may not be an obvious “gap”!!

Usually outlines the origin of the topic (e.g., seminal papers), reinforced with what others have done

May be variations on the general theme, replications in different places or with different variables or models, or exploring different functional mechanisms

Don’t forget the how: data, methods, variables

title: Literature Reviews:
section: Some questions we can ask ourselves
text:
Some questions we can ask ourselves

What questions are asked on this topic?
What do we know?
The mechanisms by which a phenomenon is hypothesized to operate and what previous research has shown
How are questions asked/answered?

Methods
Variables
Data



Are there disputes or equivocal approaches? How will you fit into these debates?

title: Literature Reviews:
section: Maybe you’re thinking: Why do I have to do this?
text:
Maybe you’re thinking: Why do I have to do this?

What we find in our research is dependent on how we framed the question in the first place

For ourselves, we want to lay out our assumptions, context, and expectations
For others, we want to help them understand where we’re coming from and why we do what we do (research question, but also methods and data!)

Knowing what has been found in previous research will help you to place your findings into a larger context later in the paper/thesis

e.g., “similar to so-and-so, we also find that X has a strong positive effect on Y”

To get ideas for model specifications, variables, possible challenges that may arise and how to avert them, interpretation of results, etc
It is not about establishing that no one has done what you’re doing ever before in history
In fact, life is much easier if you can link to some related research.

title: Literature Reviews:
section: How to get started (some ideas)
text:
How to get started (some ideas)

You’re going to need to read
A “snowball” approach can be easiest

Start with the one or two papers that you know are relevant and useful
The ones you know you would cite
Look at their references and read those (relevant) papers

Google + Google Scholar

This is not a quick approach! It requires time and skimming lots of papers until you find the good stuff!

Start to identify the main themes in your topic

Don’t organize around paper; organize around topic or theme!

title: Literature Reviews:
section: Last words of advice
text:
Last words of advice

When you take notes on a paper, keep track of what you valued it for

Foundational literature? For their methodological approach? For the niche/gap in the literature they identify?

When you find a really useful paper, have a look at their references!
Your literature review should not read like a laundry list of citations.
Have a structure in mind after you’re done reading and before you sit down to write
It’s ok to cite selectively, but be aware of who you’re including/excluding!
What if you can’t find any related research? You’ll need to be creative about establishing a broader context for your work
Keep in mind who your community of scholars is: what literatures will they be expecting you to draw from?

Exciting geographical tools

Synthetic Population Catalyst (SPC)–A synthetic population and its extended AcBM (activity-based modelling) dataset that simulates individual-level travel behaviour (homeplace and workplace), travel mode, person and socio-economic factors to allow us to explore heat vulnerability at the individual level.
Tube operation timetable–For travel times and route estimation, we use the timetable provided by TfL APIs. Provides accurate estimation whether travellers for each OD-pair will take air-conditioned Tube lines.
Clim-recal–Estimates weather and heat wave days in the past and future on a daily basis in 2.2 km*2.2 km cells covering the entire UK. Local variation in the dataset is used to estimate heat exposure more accurately.

Introducing the ESRC SDR Imagery Data Service*
1. Imagery innovation–research-ready imagery-based data products, building off and developing innovative computing and AI methods that facilitate efficient automated workflows for measures and indicators, as well as custom-defined geographies and time periods.
2. Data for all–data distribution channels that meet researchers and policymakers where they are, with user-friendly interfaces, familiar file formats, linkage and integration with existing data resources
